title: London Diaspora Stages Counter-Protest Backing Modi Outside Indian High Commission
excerpt: Supporters of the prime minister gathered at the same London site as NSUI and SFI-UK demonstrators demanding electoral integrity and the chief election commissioner's resignation.
body:
• Members of the Indian diaspora held a counter-protest outside the Indian High Commission in London on Friday in support of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the Indian government.
  • The gathering opposed demonstrations by NSUI and SFI-UK, which demanded electoral integrity and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
  • Counter-protesters said the government holds a democratic mandate and argued that raising concerns abroad should not damage India's reputation.
  • The London rallies mirrored protests in Delhi and other Indian cities over electoral roll revision and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).

Members of the Indian diaspora in London staged a counter-protest outside the Indian High Commission on Friday in support of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, as rival groups demonstrated against the Indian government nearby. According to ANI's report of the gathering, the counter-protest was directed at demonstrations by the Congress-backed National Students' Union of India (NSUI) and other like-minded groups.

A second account, published by News18, said the Students' Federation of India-UK (SFI-UK) was holding its own demonstration at the same location, demanding electoral integrity and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

What the counter-protesters said

Participants told IANS the gathering was meant to support an elected government. One diaspora member said the group had assembled because the prime minister and his government were democratically elected and had every democratic right to remain in power. Another argued that protesters could raise concerns without harming the country's standing overseas, drawing a line between standing up for one's rights and defaming India on foreign soil.

https://x.com/ANI/status/2111142667153555767

"Standing up for your rights and defaming India are two different things."

— Indian diaspora member in London, speaking to IANS

SFI-UK, for its part, said on X that its members had protested outside the High Commission and had stood firm despite attempts to disrupt their demonstration. The two gatherings took place peacefully in the accounts published so far, with each side using the same pavement to make an opposing case about the direction of Indian democracy.

The protests in India behind the London rallies

The London demonstrations were the overseas echo of a day of protests in India. In Delhi, supporters of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) and student organisations gathered around Connaught Place and Mandi House, demanding the Chief Election Commissioner's resignation, the rollback of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, and the withdrawal of the 2023 Election Commissioner Appointment Act. The SIR is the Election Commission's intensive re-verification of voter lists, which opposition parties have criticised and the Commission has defended as a routine clean-up of the rolls.

Police denied permission for the CJP's planned 'Lehra Do Tiranga' march, citing prohibitory orders in the area, and CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke was detained as he left home to join the protest. ANI reported that around 150 demonstrators were detained in central Delhi, and that Aam Aadmi Party workers also held a Tiranga rally directed at the Election Commission. Demonstrations were also reported in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Kolkata.

A familiar pattern for the UK diaspora

This is the second time in three days that the High Commission in London has been the focal point for competing diaspora demonstrations over the electoral roll issue. An earlier protest at the same site over the revision exercise drew coverage this week, and Friday's counter-protest was, in effect, the response to it: where the first gathering accused the authorities in New Delhi of undermining electoral fairness, the second insisted the government under attack had been chosen by Indian voters and deserved defending abroad.

For Britain's Indian community — one of the largest diaspora populations in the world — the episode underlines how quickly domestic Indian political arguments now travel. Campaigns over voter rolls, election appointments and institutional accountability are no longer fought only in Delhi; they are argued, in parallel, outside Indian missions in London and other diaspora capitals, often on the same day.

What to watch next

The immediate question is whether the protests in India sustain momentum after Friday's detentions, and whether opposition parties fold the SIR dispute into their wider campaign against the Election Commission. In London, further demonstrations at the High Commission are likely while the issue remains live in India. Readers in the UK following the dispute can track both sides' stated positions through the reporting linked above rather than relying on clipped social media video, which rarely shows both gatherings.
